sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Smart grids (SGs) integrate information and communication technology (ICT) into
power infrastructures to support efficient and intelligent energy management [1,2]. Com-
pared with traditional power grids, which mainly rely on centralized control and one-way
communication, SGs support bidirectional communication, distributed energy generation,
and real-time monitoring. These capabilities have enabled decentralized applications such
as peer-to-peer energy trading, vehicle-to-grid systems, and distributed energy sharing,
especially with the growing use of electric vehicles (EVs), renewable energy resources,
and smart devices [3,4]. In these settings, direct communication among users and devices is
essential for autonomous energy exchange and coordination. As SG entities communicate
more frequently, secure authentication and key agreement (AKA) mechanisms become
necessary. Applications such as user-to-user (U2U) energy trading and vehicle-to-vehicle
energy exchange require entities to authenticate each other over public channels [ 5–9],
often without relying on centralized infrastructure during communication. This creates
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 6059 https://doi.org/10.3390/app16126059
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 6059 2 of 26
several security risks, including impersonation, replay, man-in-the-middle (MITM), denial-
of-service (DoS), and privileged insider attacks [ 2,10]. Privacy is also a major concern,
since electricity consumption data can reveal users’ behaviors and lifestyles [ 11]. Thus,
decentralized SG environments require lightweight AKA protocols that can provide secure
and privacy-preserving communication with low overhead.
To address these challenges, several AKA schemes have been proposed for SG systems.
Chim et al. [12] introduced a privacy-preserving authentication scheme, while Nicanfar and
Leung [13] proposed an ECC-based AKA protocol for SG environments. Subsequent stud-
ies, including those by Odelu et al. [14], Wazid et al. [15], Gope and Sikdar [16], Hu et al. [17],
and Wu et al. [18], further improved the security and efficiency of ECC-based authentication
for resource-constrained devices. However, most existing schemes still follow a centralized
model in which a trusted authority or service provider is involved in authentication. As a
result, they are not fully suitable for decentralized SG applications, where entities must
establish trust and session keys directly over public channels without relying on online
assistance from a trusted third party. Recently, Khan et al. [ 19] proposed an ECC-based
AKA protocol for smart grid communication environments (SGAK). Although SGAK aims
to support mutual authentication and secure session-key establishment, our cryptanalysis
identifies several security weaknesses. Specifically, SGAK is vulnerable to impersonation,
ephemeral secret leakage (ESL), and DoS attacks. In addition, it does not sufficiently ensure
anonymity, untraceability, data confidentiality, or message authentication.
To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a lightweight ECC-based AKA pro-
tocol for U2U smart grid communications. In the proposed scheme, users can authenticate
each other directly and establish a secure session key without requiring a trusted authority
to participate online during authentication. The protocol is designed to resist imperson-
ation, replay, privileged insider, and ESL attacks. It also preserves user anonymity and
untraceability, making it suitable for decentralized SG applications. The main contributions
of this paper are summarized as follows:
• We analyze Khan et al.’s SGAK protocol and identify several security weaknesses,
including susceptibility to impersonation, ESL, and DoS attacks.
• We propose a lightweight ECC-based AKA protocol for decentralized communication
in smart grid environments, where users can authenticate each other without online
support from a trusted authority.
• The proposed scheme provides mutual authentication and secure session-key estab-
lishment, and is designed to resist replay, impersonation, privileged insider, and
ESL attacks.
• We validate the security and efficiency of the proposed protocol through formal and
informal security analysis, as well as simulation-based performance comparison with
existing schemes.

sections.title: 2 Related Works
sections.text:
Since Fouda et al. [20] proposed a computational Diffie–Hellman-based AKA protocol
for smart grid (SG) communication in 2011, numerous authentication and key agreement
schemes have been developed for SG environments. Although Fouda et al.’s scheme estab-
lished an early foundation for SG security, its reliance on exponential operations resulted in
relatively high computation and communication costs, limiting its applicability to resource-
constrained environments. To address privacy concerns in SG systems, Chim et al. [ 12]
introduced a privacy-preserving authentication scheme; however, the protocol does not
fully provide key agreement, mutual authentication, or perfect forward secrecy (PFS),
and may be vulnerable to impersonation and insider attacks. Subsequently, Nicanfar and
Leung [13] proposed an ECC-based key agreement protocol for access control between
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16126059
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 6059 3 of 26
home area network devices and external controllers, supporting forward and backward
confidentiality. Nevertheless, the scheme does not fully satisfy the increasing security
demands of modern SG environments.
Building on these studies, Tsai and Lo [21] proposed an anonymous key distribution
authentication scheme for SG systems and highlighted vulnerabilities in prior approaches,
including replay and impersonation attacks as well as the lack of PFS. However, subse-
quent analysis revealed that their scheme may not guarantee efficient credential privacy
for smart meters (SMs) or secure session key establishment. To overcome these limitations,
Odelu et al. [14] presented a provably secure AKA scheme with reduced computational
overhead. Despite this improvement, later studies suggested that the protocol may still
be vulnerable to impersonation and man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks and may not fully
consider the practical constraints of real SM devices. In subsequent works, Wazid et al. [15]
proposed a three-factor authentication protocol for renewable energy-based SG commu-
nication, while Abbasinezhad-Mood and Nikooghadam [ 22] introduced a lightweight
ECC-based authentication scheme suitable for practical SG environments. Gope and Sik-
dar [16] further incorporated physically unclonable functions (PUFs) [ 23,24] to enhance
privacy preservation and resistance against DoS and MITM attacks. Nevertheless, these
schemes still suffer from limitations such as incomplete anonymity support and practical
security concerns associated with fuzzy extractors.
More recently, Srinivas et al. [25] proposed an anonymous signature-based authenti-
cated key exchange scheme for IoT-enabled SG systems using Schnorr signatures, aiming
to provide anonymity and efficient key exchange; however, the scheme may not effectively
resist ESL attacks. Hu et al. [ 17] later introduced an ECC-based AKA protocol between
SMs and server virtual nodes with open-channel registration and provable security claims.
Wu et al. [ 18] subsequently demonstrated that Hu et al.’s protocol is vulnerable to key
compromise impersonation (KCI) attacks and fails to provide untraceability, and then pro-
posed a security-enhanced AKA scheme based on the elliptic curve Menezes–Qu–Vanstone
(ECMQV) mechanism. Similarly, Nkenyereye et al. [26] proposed LAP-SG, a lightweight
ECC-based authentication scheme designed for resource-constrained SM devices in large-
scale SG networks, reducing computation, communication, and storage overhead compared
with existing approaches.
Despite these advancements, existing protocols still exhibit limitations in terms of
security robustness and practical deployment efficiency. In particular, Khan et al. [ 19]
recently proposed SGAK; however, our cryptanalysis reveals that SGAK suffers from
several critical security weaknesses. Specifically, the scheme is vulnerable to impersonation,
ESL, and DoS attacks while failing to fully guarantee data confidentiality, user anonymity,
untraceability, and message authentication. These limitations motivate the design of the
proposed protocol in this work.

sections.title: 3 Preliminaries
3.1 Elliptic Curve Cryptography
sections.text:
ECC is a public-key cryptographic technique that relies on the algebraic properties
of elliptic curves defined over finite fields [27]. In comparison with conventional public-
key systems such as RSA, ECC can provide an equivalent level of security while using
significantly smaller key sizes. This characteristic makes ECC particularly appropriate for
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16126059
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 6059 4 of 26
devices with limited computational resources, such as smart meters deployed in smart
grid environments.
An elliptic curve E defined over a prime finite field Zp can be represented by the
following Weierstrass equation:
E : y2 = x3 + ax + b (mod p) (1)
where p denotes a large prime number, and a, b ∈ Zp. The curve must satisfy the non-
singularity condition 4a3 + 27b2 (mod p) ̸= 0 to ensure that it forms a valid elliptic curve.
The collection of all points satisfying the above equation, together with the point at infinity
O, constitutes an abelian group G under elliptic curve point addition, where O acts as the
identity element. Let G be a publicly known generator point of prime order q, such that
q · G = O. For an integer k ∈ Z∗
q, scalar multiplication is defined as repeated addition of
the generator point, i.e., k · G = G + G + · · ·+ G performed k times [27].
In the proposed protocol, elliptic curve scalar multiplication serves as the core opera-
tion for generating temporary key pairs and establishing shared secret values during the
authentication and key agreement procedure.
3.2. Elliptic Curve Diffie–Hellman Problem
The security of cryptographic constructions based on elliptic curves is primarily
derived from the computational difficulty of two well-known problems: the Elliptic Curve
Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP) and the Elliptic Curve Diffie–Hellman Problem
(ECDHP) [27]. The ECDLP states that, given a generator point G of prime order q and
another point Q = k · G ∈ G, it is computationally infeasible to recover the scalar value
k ∈ Z∗
q within polynomial time. Based on this assumption, the ECDHP can be described
as follows. Given two publicly known points a · G and b · G corresponding to unknown
integers a, b ∈ Z∗
q, it is computationally infeasible to compute the point a · b · G without
knowledge of either a or b. Formally, for any probabilistic polynomial-time adversary A,
the advantage of solving the ECDHP is defined as:
AdvECDHP
A = Pr[A(G, a · G, b · G) =a · b · G] ≤ ε (2)
where ε represents a negligible positive value.
In the context of this work, the hardness of the ECDLP ensures that temporary secret
values cannot be recovered from publicly exchanged parameters, whereas the hardness
of the ECDHP guarantees that the session key established through the ECDH-based key
agreement process remains secure against external adversaries.

sections.title: 3.3 Schnorr-Based Signature
sections.text:
The Schnorr signature [28] is a lightweight digital signature technique whose security
relies on the intractability of the discrete logarithm problem. It follows a three-step interac-
tion pattern consisting of a commitment, a challenge, and a response, collectively enabling
a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of a secret value.
Let G be a cyclic group of prime order q with generator point G. Assume that a
prover possesses a long-term private key σ ∈ Z∗
q and a corresponding public key X = σ · G.
To demonstrate knowledge of the secret value σ without revealing it, the prover executes
the following procedure. First, the prover selects a random nonce u ∈ Z∗
q and computes a
comMITMent M = u · G. Next, a challenge value is generated as Auth = h(M∥·), where
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16126059
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 6059 5 of 26
h(·) denotes a cryptographic hash function and the input may include session-related
parameters. Finally, the prover computes a response value:
z = u + Auth · σ (mod q) (3)
The verifier validates the correctness of the signature by checking whether
z · G ?= M + Auth · X (4)
This equality holds because
z · G = (u + Auth · σ) · G = u · G + Auth · σ · G = M + Auth · X (5)
The zero-knowledge property of this mechanism ensures that the response value z
does not reveal any information about the private key σ, since the nonce u is independently
and randomly generated for each execution.
In the proposed protocol, a Schnorr-based signature is incorporated into the authen-
tication phase to enable each smart meter to prove possession of its long-term credential
σi without exposing it over public communication channels, thereby providing protection
against credential compromise and impersonation attacks.

sections.title: 3.4 System Model
sections.text:
The proposed U2U smart grid communication environment consists of two types of
entities: users and a trusted authority (TA). Two users communicate directly with each other
over a public channel after completing the registration process with the trusted authority.
The trusted authority is responsible for managing system parameters and assisting in
the registration of users. Finally, both users establish a shared session key for secure
communication. The details of each entity are described below and illustrated in Figure 1.
Figure 1. System model.
• User (Ui): A user Ui represents a smart grid device participating in U2U communica-
tion with other registered users in the smart grid environment. The user is equipped
with communication and computation capabilities to perform authentication and
secure communication. Before initiating communication, the user must complete a
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16126059
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 6059 6 of 26
one-time registration with the trusted authority through a secure channel. After reg-
istration, the user stores necessary parameters in its device memory and performs
mutual authentication and session key establishment with other registered users over
a public channel. We assume that the user’s device may be compromised or controlled
by an adversary.
• TA: The TA is responsible for system initialization, parameter generation, and user
registration management. Specifically, the TA generates system parameters, verifies
the legitimacy of users during the registration phase, and securely distributes necessary
credentials. We assume that the trusted authority is a trusted entity and operates in a
secure environment.

sections.title: 3.5 Adversary Model
sections.text:
We employ an adversary model based on the Canetti–Krawczyk (CK) model [29] to
define the capabilities of the adversary.
The details are as follows:
• The adversary can eavesdrop on, intercept, modify, inject, delay, or replay messages
transmitted over public channels.
• The adversary can extract stored parameters from a user’s device if the device is
physically captured or compromised.
• The adversary can obtain session-specific ephemeral secrets or intermediate parame-
ters of compromised sessions.
• The adversary can launch various attacks, including impersonation, replay, and man-
in-the-middle attacks.
• The adversary may also operate as an insider within the system.

5. Cryptanalysis of Khan et al.’s Scheme
In this section, we conduct a thorough cryptanalysis of Khan et al.’s scheme and
demonstrate that it is susceptible to several security attacks. Specifically, we show that
the scheme fails to prevent impersonation attack, ESL attack, and DoS attack, and cannot
ensure data confidentiality, user anonymity, untraceability, and message authentication.
The detailed steps of each attack are described in the following subsections.

sections.title: 5.1 Impersonation Attack
sections.text:
A malicious adversary A eavesdrops on the public channel and impersonates a legiti-
mate user UA to establish a session key with UB. The detailed steps are outlined as follows.
Step 1: A intercepts the message {E1, T1} transmitted from UA to UB over the public
channel. Since PKB, XA, and T1 are all public values, A can directly compute
K1 = h(PKB∥XA∥T1).
Step 2: A decrypts E1 using K1 to obtain ID A1 and MA. Then, A recovers the real identity
of UA by computing ID A = ID A1 ⊕ h(MA∥PK∥T1).

sections.title: 5.2 Ephemeral Secret Leakage Attack
sections.text:
A malicious adversary A assumes that the ephemeral secret b has been leaked and
combines it with information obtained by eavesdropping on the public channel to fully
recover the session key SKB. The detailed steps are outlined as follows.
Step 1: A computes K1 = h(PKB∥XA∥T1) using the public values PKB, XA, and T1,
and decrypts the intercepted E1 to obtain ID A1 and MA. Then, A recovers the
real identity of UA by computing ID A = ID A1 ⊕ h(MA∥PK∥T1).
Step 2: A computes K2 = h(MA∥T3∥ID ∗
A) using MA, ID A, and T3, and decrypts the
intercepted E2 to obtain ID B, N, and MB.
Step 3: Once b is leaked, A can fully recover the session key by computing b · a · g = b ·
MA, and thus derives SKB = h(ID ∗
A∥ID B∥N∥MA∥MB∥b · a · g∥T3). This directly
contradicts Khan et al.’s security claim that both the long-term and ephemeral
secrets must be known to compute the session key.

sections.title: 5.3 Data Confidentiality Violation
sections.text:
Khan et al.’s scheme claims that data confidentiality is guaranteed by encrypting E1
with K1 = h(PKB∥XA∥T1). However, since PKB, XA, and T1 are all public values exposed
over the public channel, any adversary A can directly compute K1 and decrypt E1 to
obtain ID A1 and MA. Similarly, K2 = h(MA∥T3∥ID A) can also be computed using the
previously obtained MA and the public values T3 and ID A, allowing A to decrypt E2 as
well. Consequently, Khan et al.’s claim that “an adversary cannot decrypt the messages”
does not hold.

sections.title: 5.4 User Anonymity and Untraceability Violation
sections.text:
Khan et al.’s scheme claims that user anonymity and untraceability are guaranteed
since UA transmits its anonymous identity ID A1 in encrypted form. However, since all
values composing K1 = h(PKB∥XA∥T1), namely PKB, XA, and T1, are exposed over the
public channel, A can directly compute K1, decrypt E1, and recover the real identity ID A.
Furthermore, by repeatedly recovering ID A from different sessions using the same method,
A can determine that those sessions originated from the same user. Therefore, both user
anonymity and untraceability do not hold in Khan et al.’s scheme.

sections.title: 5.5 Message Unauthentication
sections.text:
Khan et al.’s scheme claims that message authentication is guaranteed through times-
tamp and hash value verification. However, when UB receives E1, it only checks the
validity of the timestamp and has no means to verify whether the message actually orig-
inated from UA. Therefore, even if A transmits a forged message, UB accepts it as a
legitimate message from UA. Consequently, Khan et al.’s scheme fails to guarantee message
origin authentication.

sections.title: 6 Proposed Scheme
sections.text:
In this section, we propose a mutual authentication and key agreement protocol
for U2U smart grid communication based on elliptic curve cryptography. The proposed
scheme consists of four phases: system initialization, registration, authentication and key
agreement, and re-authentication. The flowcharts of each phase are illustrated in the
corresponding figures.

sections.title: 6.1 Initialization Phase
sections.text:
Before the registration phase, the trusted authority (TA) establishes the system param-
eters as follows. The TA selects an elliptic curve E over a finite field Fp with a base point g
of prime order q, chooses a master secret key s, and computes the corresponding public
key Ps = s · g. The TA also selects a secure one-way hash function h(·) and publishes the
system parameters {E, g, q, h(·), Ps} over a public channel, while keeping s secret.

sections.title: 6.2 Registration Phase
sections.text:
Before participating in the authentication process, each user Ui must complete a one-
time registration with the TA through a secure channel. The detailed process is outlined
below and illustrated in Figure 3.
User Ui Trusted Authority TA
Input IDi, PWi
Selects ni, xi

sections.title: 7.1 Formal Analysis Using AVISP A
sections.text:
To further validate the robustness of the proposed authentication protocol, formal
security verification is conducted using the AVISPA (Automated Validation of Internet
Security Protocols and Applications) tool [30]. AVISPA is a well-established framework
for the automated analysis of cryptographic protocols and is widely utilized to examine
whether security protocols satisfy their intended authentication and confidentiality require-
ments under adversarial environments. The platform supports systematic exploration
of potential protocol weaknesses against a variety of attack models. The proposed pro-
tocol is specified using the High-Level Protocol Specification Language (HLPSL), which
enables formal modeling of protocol entities, communication procedures, and security
objectives. Through HLPSL, authentication and secrecy goals can be explicitly represented
and analyzed in a mathematically rigorous manner. The HLPSL description is subsequently
translated into the Intermediate Format (IF) by the HLPSL2IF translator, allowing the
protocol to be evaluated by multiple automated verification backends. To obtain a compre-
hensive assessment, the protocol is analyzed using several backend verification engines
supported by AVISPA, including the On-the-Fly Model Checker (OFMC), the Constraint-
Logic-based Attack Searcher (CL-AtSE), the SAT-based Model Checker (SATMC), and the
Tree Automata-based Protocol Analyzer (TA4SP). Since each backend adopts different
search strategies and verification methodologies, the combined analysis improves the
reliability and completeness of the security evaluation.
For the experimental verification, simulations are carried out using the OFMC and CL-
AtSE backends. As illustrated in Figure 6, both analyzers return a SAFE status, indicating
that no attack violating the specified authentication and secrecy goals is found under
the considered Dolev–Yao adversarial model. For OFMC, the protocol analysis explores

sections.text:
message-exchange steps considered during state-space exploration, and completes in 0.54 s.
For CL-AtSe, 68 protocol states are analyzed and no attack state is found. These statistics
indicate that the protocol is systematically explored within the considered state space
without revealing any feasible attack path. Therefore, the AVISPA results confirm that
the proposed protocol satisfies the desired security goals and can successfully withstand

and man-in-the-middle attacks.

sections.title: 7.2 Formal Analysis Using the RoR Model
sections.text:
To evaluate the session key security of the proposed authentication protocol, this
paper employs the Real-or-Random (RoR) security model [31]. The RoR model provides
a formal framework for analyzing whether an adversary can successfully distinguish a
legitimately established session key from a randomly selected value. By adopting this
model, the resistance of the proposed protocol against session key disclosure attacks can
be systematically examined. In the considered framework, each communicating party
is modeled as an instance denoted by pt, where p identifies the protocol entity and t
specifies the corresponding session instance. During the security experiment, the adversary
A is allowed to interact with protocol participants through a set of oracle queries in
order to gain knowledge about the generated session key. Moreover, the adversary is
assumed to possess full control over the public communication channel, enabling both
passive attacks, including message interception, and active attacks, such as replay, injection,
and modification of transmitted messages. The detailed query capabilities available to the
adversary in the RoR model are summarized in Table 2. Furthermore, | Hash | represents
the cardinality of the output space of the hash functionH(·), while qh denotes the maximum
number of hash queries that adversary A can perform during the security game.
